content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, 'wings' (Hebrew kanaph) most commonly symbolizes God's protective care, refuge, and covering — the believer finds shelter 'under the shadow of his wings,' with the image drawn from a mother bird (especially an eagle or hen) sheltering her young. It expresses divine protection, tenderness, and covenantal safekeeping.","primary_basis":["Psalm 91:4 ('He will cover you with his feathers, and under his wings you will find refuge')","Psalm 17:8 ('hide me in the shadow of your wings')","Psalm 36:7; Psalm 57:1; Psalm 61:4; Psalm 63:7 (refuge in the shadow of God's wings)","Ruth 2:12 ('the LORD... under whose wings you have come to take refuge')","Deuteronomy 32:11 (eagle stirring its nest, spreading its wings over its young)","Exodus 19:4 ('I carried you on eagles' wings')","Matthew 23:37 / Luke 13:34 (Jesus: 'as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings')"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The corner/edge of a garment as a symbol of covenant covering, marriage, or redemption — since kanaph also means the hem or corner of a robe, spreading one's 'wing' over someone signifies taking them into covenant protection (as Boaz over Ruth, or God over Israel).","basis":["Ruth 3:9 ('spread the corner [kanaph] of your garment over your servant')","Ezekiel 16:8 (God spreads the corner of his garment over Jerusalem in covenant)","Numbers 15:38 and Deuteronomy 22:12 (tassels on the corners/kanaph of garments)","1 Samuel 24:4-5 (David cuts the corner of Saul's robe)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Healing and messianic restoration — 'the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings,' often read christologically; some interpreters connect it to the woman healed by touching the fringe (on the kanaph) of Jesus' garment.","basis":["Malachi 4:2","Matthew 9:20-21 and 14:36 (touching the fringe/hem of Jesus' garment)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Angelic/cherubic wings signifying the presence, holiness, and mobility of God's heavenly attendants and the mercy seat as the place of divine presence.","basis":["Exodus 25:20 (cherubim wings over the mercy seat)","Isaiah 6:2 (seraphim with six wings)","Ezekiel 1 and 10 (winged living creatures)","1 Kings 8:6-7 (cherubim wings in the temple)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Strength, swiftness, and divine empowerment or deliverance — soaring 'on wings like eagles' as renewed strength, or God riding 'on the wings of the wind' as swift intervention.","basis":["Isaiah 40:31","Psalm 18:10; Psalm 104:3 (wings of the wind)","2 Samuel 22:11"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The extremities or 'ends/corners' of the earth or land — kanaph used geographically to denote the farthest edges.","basis":["Isaiah 24:16 ('from the ends [kanaph] of the earth')","Job 37:3; Job 38:13","Isaiah 11:12 ('four corners of the earth')"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"Kanaph is polysemous in Hebrew, covering both a bird's wing and the corner/edge of a garment or the land, so its symbolic range is broader than the English word 'wing' suggests. Nevertheless, there is a clear and widely recognized consensus in Christian devotional, homiletical, and scholarly literature that the primary symbolic use is divine protection and refuge, reinforced by Jesus' own hen-and-chicks image, which is generally treated as continuous with the Old Testament motif. The garment-corner/covenant reading and the Malachi 'healing in his wings' reading are well established secondary strands, particularly in messianic and Hebraic-roots teaching, but they do not displace the protection motif as the dominant interpretation."}
